lesson.title: From Name to Formula: Balancing the Charges
lesson.summary: Writing an ionic formula from a compound's name means figuring out each ion's charge and then combining the smallest whole-number ratio of ions that makes the total charge exactly zero.
lesson.body:
Naming an ionic compound starts from its formula and ends at a name; writing a formula runs that process in reverse, starting from the name and ending at a formula. The underlying rule is always the same: every ionic compound must be electrically neutral overall, so the positive charge contributed by all the cations must exactly cancel the negative charge contributed by all the anions. Writing a correct formula is really just an exercise in finding the smallest whole-number ratio of ions that satisfies that balance.

Start with the simple cases, where the ratio is easy to see by inspection. Potassium bromide pairs K+ with Br-, a 1-to-1 ratio, giving KBr. Calcium chloride pairs Ca2+ with Cl-, and since one chloride only cancels one unit of calcium's 2+ charge, two chloride ions are needed, giving CaCl2. The subscript 2 applies only to chlorine, since chlorine is a single-element ion here, no parentheses required.

Polyatomic ions need one extra formatting rule: whenever more than one of a polyatomic ion is required, the ion's formula is enclosed in parentheses with the subscript placed outside them, so the subscript is understood to multiply the entire ion rather than just its last atom. Calcium nitrate pairs Ca2+ with NO3-, and balancing 2+ against 1- requires two nitrate ions, written as Ca(NO3)2, not CaNO32, which would incorrectly suggest 32 oxygen atoms. Ammonium sulfate pairs NH4+ with SO4 2-, and balancing 1+ against 2- requires two ammonium ions, written as (NH4)2SO4.

Some pairings need a genuine common-multiple calculation rather than simple doubling. Calcium phosphate pairs Ca2+ with PO4 3-. Charges of 2 and 3 do not cancel at a 1-to-1 or even a 1-to-2 ratio, so find the lowest common multiple of 2 and 3, which is 6: three calcium ions contribute 6+, and two phosphate ions contribute 6-, giving the formula Ca3(PO4)2. Aluminum sulfate works the same way, pairing Al3+ with SO4 2-: the lowest common multiple of 3 and 2 is again 6, requiring two aluminum ions and three sulfate ions, giving Al2(SO4)3.

The same logic applies without modification to variable-charge metals once the Roman numeral in the name specifies which charge is in play. Iron(III) oxide names Fe3+ explicitly, so it pairs against O2- using the common multiple of 3 and 2, which is 6, requiring two iron ions and three oxide ions, Fe2O3. Iron(II) oxide, by contrast, names Fe2+, which pairs 1-to-1 with O2-, giving FeO, a completely different compound. Reading the Roman numeral correctly is therefore not optional decoration, it is the piece of information that determines the entire ratio and formula that follows.

One common mistake is worth watching for: a crisscross shortcut, where the numeral value of the cation's charge is dropped straight in as the anion's subscript and vice versa, can produce a formula that is not actually reduced to its lowest whole-number ratio. Magnesium oxide is the clearest case. Crisscrossing Mg2+ and O2- naively gives Mg2O2, but 2-to-2 is not the lowest whole-number ratio, it is just 1-to-1 written with an unnecessary common factor of two still attached, so the ratio must be reduced down to the correct formula, MgO. The same reduction applies any time both charges share a common factor, for instance tin(IV) sulfide, pairing Sn4+ with S2-, reduces from a raw 2-to-4 crisscross down to SnS2. Always check whether the subscripts you land on share a common factor before calling a formula finished.
